key_messages: Dry weather with above normal temperatures continues through the end of the week.

The weekend will be unseasonably warm and primarily dry. By Sunday evening, chances for rain increase associated with a possible east coast storm. Then a strong front will bring much colder conditions to the region later Monday into Tuesday.

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
202 PM EST Tue Nov 17 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 201 PM EST Tuesday...

No significant changes were made with this forecast package.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 201 PM EST Tuesday...

1. Dry weather with above normal temperatures continues through 
the end of the week.  

2. The weekend will be unseasonably warm and primarily dry. By 
Sunday evening, chances for rain increase associated with a 
possible east coast storm. Then a strong front will bring much 
colder conditions to the region later Monday into Tuesday.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 201 PM EST Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A large area of high pressure will maintain generally 
quiet weather across the area through the end of the work week. 
Temperatures will run 5-10 degrees above normal through Friday. 
Highs will generally range through the 50s and lows will 
range through the 30s into low 40s.  

The center of the surface high will remain to our south, which will 
maintain a pressure gradient over our area that will support some 
light west to southwest winds at the surface, with occasional gusts 
to around 15 mph possible each afternoon. Higher elevations, 
especially over northern NY, will see higher gusts. Gusts over the 
northern Adirondacks will generally be in the 15 to 25 mph range, 
though higher summits will see gusts in excess of 40 mph at times. 
These breezes, along with some overnight cloud cover as shortwaves 
move through, will prevent ideal radiational cooling conditions and 
will keep lows seasonably mild.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Dry conditions are near certain to continue through 
Sunday morning, with near record daily high temperatures anticipated 
at long term climate sites. Sunday will mark six consecutive warm 
days across the region. Thereafter, increasing chances of rain, 
especially beginning Sunday evening into Monday, will be tied to two 
systems that will generally converge towards our region. Through 
early next week, while the risk of impactful weather is low, a more 
active pattern will begin regardless of how things play out. 

There are generally three scenarios that model solutions fall into 
for this period; a mainly dry one, a light rain event with perhaps 
some higher terrain snow showers in the wake of a cold front, or a 
moderate rainfall favored in southern/eastern portions of the 
region. This latter, more noteworthy outcome would occur if low 
pressure developing later this week forms farther west than the 
consensus across Florida, which leads to a track hugging the east 
coast rather than out to sea. The latest run of the GEFS strongly 
favors an out to sea scenario, but its operational run and many 
members of the ECMWF EPS and AIFS systems still show a risk of this 
wetter scenario. 

The most likely outcome is in the official forecast, which shows 
some rain showers associated with an incoming cold front from the 
west that will put an end to our unseasonable warmth. The character 
of this front is hard to pin down right now; a sharper front could 
induce some relatively heavy showers and a changeover to snow by 
Tuesday morning. Otherwise, would expect no impacts with 
precipitation amounts under 0.25" and more likely under 0.1" in most 
locations. The final scenario is almost entirely dry with both a 
miss in the coastal storm and a cold front that produces little 
precipitation as low pressure weakens to our north as it passes 
through Monday.

&&

.AVIATION /19Z TUESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Through 18Z Wednesday...VFR should prevail through the TAF period at
all terminals with only high altitude clouds present, with the
possible exception at SLK. Here, some upslope moisture transport
overnight could bring a brief period where an MVFR cloud deck
develops; such clouds if they form are favored to dissipate within a
few hours with low (under 20%) chance of ceilings below 1000 feet.
A modest and broad surface trough, along with the passage of a
shortwave trough this evening, will promote enough
westerly/southwesterly winds to bring some LLWS concerns to more
mountainous areas such that SLK and EFK will reach likely reach
criteria at times overnight and into early Wednesday. Otherwise,
gusts at MSS and SLK near 20 knots will abate towards 21Z and pick
back up within a few hours of sunrise to similar magnitudes.
Elsewhere surface winds will be mainly under 10 knots through the
period.

Outlook...

Thursday: VFR. NO SIG WX.

Friday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. NO SIG WX.
Saturday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Saturday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Sunday: VFR. Slight chance RA.
